extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy/psychology, educators, and researchers interested in methods for investigating human character and mental phenomena
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and methodological criteria for investigating the formation of character (ethology) — how to derive laws of character from elementary laws of mind, and the limits of experiment and observation in doing so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary laws of mind (laws of association)
rubrics_metrics.description: These simple or elementary Laws of Mind have been ascertained by the ordinary methods of experimental inquiry; (earlier enumerated laws govern how ideas excite one another: contiguity, frequency of conjunction, and intensity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elementary laws are the basis from which more complex laws of thought and feeling are generated. They were obtained experimentally and serve as the foundational principles for subsequent deductive work in ethology. (The text refers readers to psychological works where these laws and applications are exemplified.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental chemistry vs composition of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: When many impressions or ideas operate together they sometimes 'melt and coalesce' into one another so as to appear not several ideas but one; in such cases the complex idea should be said to 'result from', or 'be generated by', the simple ideas, not to 'consist' of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the distinction when analysing complex mental phenomena: e.g., seven prismatic colours in rapid succession 'generate' white (they are not themselves white); an 'orange' really 'consists' of distinguishable simple ideas. This affects how we attribute origins to complex mental states and when we must study the complex state in its own right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement insufficient; require Method of Difference to prove causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing that B and C were or may have been present whenever A (a complex mental feeling) was found amounts only to the Method of Agreement and cannot prove causation until confirmed by the more conclusive Method of Difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When testing whether association generates a complex mental state (e.g., belief or moral reprobation), one must not rely solely on correlative coincidence; one must also test whether introducing or removing the candidate cause changes the effect (the Method of Difference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Even when generated from simpler laws, complex phenomena require direct experimental study
rubrics_metrics.description: The generation of one class of mental phenomena from another, whenever made out, is interesting but 'no more supersedes the necessity of an experimental study of the generated phenomenon' than knowing oxygen and sulphur lets us deduce properties of sulphuric acid without specific observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that deducing a complex phenomenon from simpler principles eliminates the need to observe and experiment on the complex phenomenon itself; identify its own sequences and laws empirically as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for bodily/organic states influencing mental phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquiries must examine 'how far the production of one state of mind by another is influenced by any assignable state of body' — differences in mental susceptibility may be original, the result of prior mental history, or depend on varieties of physical organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish causes that are psychological (history, association) from those that are organic. Consider examples (nervous susceptibility intensifying pleasurable sensation, thereby intensifying desire) and avoid attributing psychological effects directly to physiology when they may act via altered sensations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical laws are approximate generalizations and limited to observed circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: An Empirical Law is an uniformity true in instances within our observation but not of a nature to afford assurance it would hold beyond those limits; it depends on more general conditions and may be resolvable into simpler sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat common maxims (e.g., 'the old are cautious') as empirical generalizations that require explanation by causal laws before being extrapolated to other times, places, or populations. Always ask 'why is it true?' and seek underlying causes to evaluate applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve empirical laws into causal laws to determine limits of reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The really scientific truths are not the empirical laws but the causal laws which explain them; empirical laws derive whatever truth they have from causing principles and must be resolved into them to know their limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use causal analysis to assess how far an empirical generalization will hold in different contexts (e.g., national character changes under altered institutions). Verification of empirical laws requires showing they follow from known causes that extend to the case in question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive method is required for studying formation of character (Ethology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because character and the aggregate circumstances forming it are of high complexity, the Deductive Method — setting out from general laws and verifying consequences by specific experience — is alone applicable for ascertaining laws of the formation of character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethology should proceed by deducing derivative laws (tendencies) from the general laws of mind (psychology), hypothesizing what character a given set of circumstances will produce, and then using observation as verification rather than attempting direct experimental control of entire life-histories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical impossibility of controlled experiments on formation of character
rubrics_metrics.description: To study formation of character by direct experiment would require bringing up and educating numerous humans from infancy with complete records of every sensation and impression — practically impossible and liable to be vitiated by a single overlooked circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the infeasibility of full experimental control in human development; this motivates the deductive approach and caution in interpreting imperfect natural 'experiments'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of observation: need many instances and control for confounders
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations can only be made 'in a rough way, and en masse'; conclusions from observation are comparative results requiring sufficiently numerous and varied instances to eliminate chance and coincident similarities of circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using observational data about character (e.g., comparing nations or groups), design comparisons to control for confounders and obtain large samples; be cautious about inferring kinds rather than differences in ratios and degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific propositions in ethology should assert tendencies, not certainties
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethological propositions must be hypothetical, affirm tendencies, not facts: 'They must not assert that something will always, or certainly, happen; but only that such and such will be the effect of a given cause, so far as it operates uncounteracted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame laws as tendencies (e.g., 'bodily strength tends to make men courageous') and acknowledge possible counteracting influences; this keeps claims scientifically modest and applicable across complex conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use knowledge of tendencies for practical shaping of circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Even imperfect knowledge of causes can be of great practical value: 'It is enough that we know that certain means have a tendency to produce a given effect... When the circumstances of an individual or of a nation are in any considerable degree under our control, we may ... shape those circumstances in a manner much more favourable to the ends we desire.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply ethological insights to education and policy as the 'art of education' — use tendencies as guides to manipulate circumstances to achieve desirable character outcomes, while recognizing limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synchronous versus successive associations shape mental types
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensations received simultaneously favour associations constituting knowledge of objects and perception of qualities; sensations received successively favour knowledge of events and ratiocinative intellect; hence different associative orders produce different types of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or designing formative experiences, consider whether stimuli are presented synchronously or successively, since this influences whether a mind develops perceptive/tasteful qualities or a philosophic/ratiocinative bent (example: synchronous impressions favour perception of objects and taste; successive impressions favour knowledge of events and reasoning).
